evidence_set: Studies requiring more than 72 hours of abstinence before testing (k = 15; n = 928) found d −0.08 (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07; P = .29), smaller than studies requiring 72 hours or less, none included (k = 54; n = 7,799; d −0.30, −0.37 to −0.22); chi-square 6.36, P = .01. Longer mean reported abstinence (k = 28; n = 1,661) went with smaller differences (beta 0.059; P = .04, uncorrected; unit of the beta not stated). Figure 3 also plots the studies requiring no abstinence (k = 22) and 1 to 72 hours (k = 32) separately, to show that the zero or unknown abstinence studies do not drive the difference. A comparison between studies, not a change within the same people; the more-than-72-hours interval includes no difference and reaches −0.22, close to the overall estimate of −0.25, which lies just outside it.

Second-hand (narrative review): studies of long-term effects rely mainly on retrospective self-report by people who chose to use cannabis; long-term memory impairments have been reported mainly in frequent, heavy use, and confounders (ability before use, alcohol and other drugs, type of cannabis, age at onset, and mental health problems including depression and problem cannabis use) make cause and effect hard to establish. Case-control studies are called inconsistent; the most consistent finding is poorer encoding of new episodic memories, with persisting deficits in some studies over the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of deficits at 28 days (as summarised from a review, ref. 25); working memory, attention and impulsivity findings are mixed; one study found no difference in decision making or risk taking against controls matched for mental-health confounds, although in that study poorer decision-making accuracy went with more symptoms of problem cannabis use (ref. 35).
